$comment: Canonical viewpoints captured by `npm run shots` and diffed by `npm run shots:check`. Every entry is forced to hud=0&panel=0&freeze=1, because a visible HUD shows fps and heap and could never match between runs. Add a view per phase; never remove one without saying why in PROGRESS.md.

views.name: cube-default
views.expect: Default seed, three seconds of sim, camera near the ground. The baseline every phase is compared against.

views.name: cube-t0
views.expect: Sim tick zero, cube unrotated. Proves ?time= seeks rather than just pausing. Chunks are static, so the cube is the only thing that may differ from cube-default.

views.name: cube-seed-alpha
views.expect: Different seed: both the cube colour and every chunk colour change. Proves seed plumbing reaches content at every tier.

views.name: cube-wireframe
views.expect: Wireframe mode on from the URL, applied to the cube and to streamed chunk meshes.

views.name: cube-far
views.expect: Camera placed entirely from the URL, far from the default framing.

views.name: chunks-aerial
views.expect: Phase 1. Looking down on the streamed chunk grid from 300m. Every 64m cell is a flat colour derived from hash2i(coord, seed); a wrong colour or a missing cell is visible instantly.

views.name: chunks-aerial-seed-beta
views.expect: Phase 1. Same viewpoint, different seed. The grid layout is identical and every colour differs, which is what proves the seed reaches the chunk generator inside the worker.

views.name: chunks-radius-edge
views.expect: Phase 1, repurposed by Phase 2b. It used to frame the edge of the 512m streaming disc against the sky; with a 4km quadtree there is no such edge to see, so what it now tests is a mid-pitch view over several level boundaries at once. Its params are deliberately unchanged -- editing a canonical viewpoint destroys the only history the harness has.

views.name: chunks-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 1. Wireframe over streamed chunks. Guards renderer.invalidateMaterials(): meshes added at runtime are invisible to wireframe mode without it, and this view goes blank if that call is lost.

views.name: chunks-far-from-origin
views.expect: Phase 1. 200km from the origin, at chunk (3200, -2048). Proves the coordinate hash and chunk-local vertex positions survive large coordinates rather than degenerating into repeats or float mush.

views.name: terrain-mountain-profile
views.expect: Phase 2a. A mountain range in silhouette against the sky, 3.3km west of the origin on the default seed. This is the view that shows the height field is doing all four of its jobs at once: a continent shelf under it, a ridged multifractal peak, hillside relief, and slope/altitude colouring with a snow cap. If the terrain regresses to noise or to a plane, this view is the first to say so.

views.name: terrain-wireframe-relief
views.expect: Phase 2a. The same viewpoint in wireframe: the 32x32 (2m) triangle grid draped over real relief. Catches a change to SEGMENTS, a broken vertex grid, or a chunk that failed to build, none of which are obvious in the shaded view. Also re-tests the coordinate-derived renderOrder now that neighbouring chunks are no longer coplanar.

views.name: lod-horizon
views.expect: Phase 2b. THE SHALLOW-PITCH VIEW, and the reason it exists: every earlier canonical view is pitched down far enough that frustum culling throws most of the world away, so none of them can show what a 4 km quadtree actually costs or what its level boundaries look like. Here the camera is 5 degrees below the horizon with the snow-capped range 2-4 km out, so all five levels in play are on screen at once. Any crack at a level boundary shows as a sliver of clear colour through the ground; the skirts are what stop that. ~97 draw calls at 1080p against a budget of 1200.

views.name: lod-ground-horizon
views.expect: Phase 2b. The same terrain from 8 m above the ground, looking 1 degree below the horizon. This is where the lod-0/lod-1 boundary lands closest to the camera (about 320 m) and therefore where a crack would be widest in screen space. It also exercises the near-plane end of the depth range against 4 km of terrain, which is what the camera's near/far change was for.

views.name: lod-rings-wireframe
views.expect: Phase 2b. Straight down from 2.6 km, in wireframe: the quadtree's structure itself. The bright centre is lod 0, whose 2 m cells are sub-pixel at this scale and so read as solid fill; each step outward doubles the node size and halves the apparent line density. The stepped boundaries are the quadtree staircase. If the selection ever collapses to a single level, inverts, or stops tiling, this is the view that says so instantly -- and nothing else in the harness would.
